description: Cross-binding conformance for esm-spec §6.6.2 'Unrecognized override keys': every `parameter_overrides` key must designate exactly ONE parameter of the flattened system, and a key that designates none is an ERROR — not a silently-ignored no-op. Three outcomes are pinned, and they are DISTINCT: a key that resolves (exactly, or by the local spelling §6.6 mandates) runs; a BARE key that is the local name of two or more parameters is AMBIGUOUS; anything else is UNKNOWN. Ambiguous is kept apart from unknown because the fixes differ — qualify the name versus correct it — and because silently binding one of two candidates would be a wrong answer rather than a missing one. Rust already raised `SimulateError::InvalidParameter` for the unknown case; Julia and Python silently ignored it, so an author's override did nothing and the run still reported a verdict. This category is what keeps the three from drifting apart again: unlike the other categories it compares DIAGNOSTIC OUTCOMES, not numbers, so it carries no golden — each binding's runner asserts its own idiomatic error type per case. NOTE on rule 2 (the dotted-suffix rule): every binding's `esm_problem` FLATTENS, so a key whose leading segments name real components is an exact hit here and rule 2's POSITIVE path is not expressible in a shared fixture — it fires only inside a binding that keeps a model's own names (Rust's single-model array build, which carries a mounted subsystem parameter as `sub.g`), and is gated there by each binding's `P.sub.g` subsystem-override test. What this category DOES pin about rule 2 is its GUARD: a key whose leading segments name no component or subsystem is UNKNOWN, never suffix-matched.

scope_excluded.go: rewrite-only port; no simulator, so no override-key surface
scope_excluded.typescript: rewrite-only port; no simulator, so no override-key surface

error_surface._comment: The idiomatic error each binding raises per outcome. The TYPE is per-language; the OUTCOME classification is the cross-binding contract.

cases.note: Exact hit on the flattening-qualified name.
The LOCAL spelling §6.6 mandates, unique across the document. The non-vacuity anchor: a binding that rejected every bare key would fail here.

A DOTTED key whose longest dotted suffix IS a parameter name (`Left.solo`), but whose LEADING SEGMENT names no component or subsystem of this document — there is no `Doc`. Rule 2 validates every segment it drops, so a mistyped qualifier is not silently discarded: `Missng.M.pert_amp` is reported instead of quietly driving `M.pert_amp`. This case USED TO RESOLVE, binding `Left.solo`; pinning it UNKNOWN is the deliberate behaviour change that makes a typo'd qualifier visible. The legitimate rule-2 spelling — the esm-spec §4.6 fully-qualified `P.sub.g` against a build carrying `sub.g`, where `P` names the model and `sub` the mounted subsystem — is unaffected, because both leading segments name something real.
Two components carry this local name; binding either would be a wrong answer.

A DOTTED key resolves only under rule 2, which needs one of its dotted suffixes to be a parameter name outright; the only suffix here is `solo`, and the parameter is `Left.solo`, not `solo`, so rule 2 fails. Rule 3 is for BARE keys only, so the qualifier is never discarded and `Missing.solo` does not quietly become `Left.solo` — an author who names a component that does not exist is told so.

fixtures._trajectory_comment: `Left.x` integrates (Left.gain + Left.solo) and `Right.y` integrates Right.gain, both from 0 over [0,1], so a resolved override is VISIBLE at t=1 and a binding that accepted a key without actually binding it is caught too. The RHS is constant, so every solver reproduces these within the manifest tolerance.
